item.title: Reading Abilities and Visual Evoked Potentials in Hearing-Impaired Children: A Comparative Study of Cochlear Implant and Hearing Aid Users.
item.description:
Audiology & neuro-otology
INTRODUCTION: This study aimed to evaluate reading comprehension skills, visual evoked potentials (VEP), and saccadic eye movements in hearing aid (HA) users, cochlear implant (CI) users, and individuals with normal hearing (NH), to investigate the relationship between sensory processing and reading ability. METHODS: The study included 45 participants, 15 HA users, 15 CI users, and 15 NH. VEP, a saccadic test, and a reading comprehension test were performed. VEP recordings were conducted with and without the hearing device for HA and CI users. RESULTS: Reading comprehension scores in the CI group were significantly lower than those in the NH and HA groups (p < 0.001). Rightward saccade velocity was consistently lower than leftward velocity across all groups. Notably, VEP amplitudes in HA users (N1-P1: p = 0.048) and CI users (N1-P1: p = 0.005, 0.019, 0.001; P1-N2: p = 0.010, 0.008, 0.022) were significantly larger in the unaided condition (without device) compared to the aided condition. Correlation analyses did not reveal a consistent pattern of association between reading comprehension scores and VEP parameters. CONCLUSION: While reading skills were found to be weaker in the CI group, the absence of a direct correlation between VEP/saccadic parameters and reading scores suggests that lower level sensory processing and higher order reading comprehension may operate through distinct mechanisms. The increased VEP amplitudes observed without hearing devices suggest a cross-modal neuroplastic compensation in the visual cortex during auditory deprivation.

item.title: Quantity and quality of children's screen use and their neural and associated behavioral outcomes: A systematic review.
item.description:
Child development
The developmental impact of screen use on young children remains an active area of inquiry, with evidence of both risks and benefits depending on quantity and quality of exposure. This systematic review synthesized 23 neuroimaging studies of children aged 0-8 years, selected from 19,699 records identified across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and APA PsycINFO (2012-2025). Studies were included if they examined typically developing children, employed neuroimaging methods (EEG, fNIRS, or MRI), and assessed the effects of digital media exposure or intervention on brain and associated outcomes. Eight studies on quantity associated greater screen exposure with lower prefrontal activation, altered cortical activity, differences in white matter pathways, and lower myelination in language and cognitive regions. Fifteen studies on quality found that interactive and multimodal media, educational gamification, and caregiver co-use enhanced networks supporting language, perception, and socioemotional skills, whereas non-educational media showed null effects. Our paper argues that discussions on screen use should move beyond the sole focus on duration of screen-time to consider the dimensions of design, content, and context of media use and how they may shape developmental outcomes.

item.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels.
item.description:
eLife
Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse's contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

item.title: Timing and meaning in spoken thought relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
When people think aloud, their reports vary in duration and in how closely successive thoughts are related in meaning. We asked whether these two dimensions relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics. Using 10-minute think-aloud fMRI scans from 75 adults, we quantified timing as variability in sentence-event duration and semantic continuity as similarity between adjacent grouped thoughts. In models including both measures, greater duration variability was associated with lower relative brain entropy (BEN), estimated from BOLD time series, in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (voxel wise FDR q < 0.05). This association persisted after adjustment for speech coverage, pause duration, articulation rate and event count. Semantic continuity was associated with differences in BOLD amplitude and synchrony across bilateral sensorimotor regions. These voxel wise associations fell below the FDR threshold after adjustment for speech coverage or pause duration. In a secondary atlas-based analysis, semantic continuity remained positively associated with local synchrony in Default C after adjustment for speech timing (β = 0.517, P = 0.003). These findings link the timing of spoken reports to dorsolateral prefrontal brain activity irregularity and show how the sensorimotor correlates of semantic continuity covary with speech timing.

item.title: Distinct developmental organization of intrinsic brain dynamics supports different components of inhibitory control during adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescent inhibitory control develops within a changing organization of intrinsic brain activity, yet the signal properties and cortical systems associated with different control demands remain unclear. We studied 101 youths aged 8-18 years using brain entropy (BEN), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Voxelwise and seven-network models evaluated age associations and task-by-age interactions while adjusting for sex, head motion, and gray-matter anatomy. Spatially standardized ALFF showed age associations in somatomotor and salience/ventral-attention networks. Contextual control, assessed with the AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), showed the broadest age-dependent coupling: all four spatially standardized measures yielded voxelwise interactions surviving permutation-based cluster false discovery rate correction, and the frontoparietal BEN interaction survived network correction. Better action cancellation was associated with higher frontoparietal BEN without a corrected network age interaction. Independent cortical references further differentiated these patterns: raw BEN age-effect evidence was stronger toward association cortex, whereas the ALFF-AX-CPT age interaction was stronger toward sensorimotor cortex. Additional task interactions aligned with the second and third connectivity gradients. Core voxelwise AX-CPT findings persisted after age trimming. These findings link the differentiation of inhibitory-control demands to the developmental organization of complementary intrinsic signal properties across cortical systems, highlighting contextual control as a prominent locus of age-dependent brain-behavior coupling.

item.title: Beyond morphometry: Adolescent brain microarchitecture reflects sex differences in pubertal timing and hormones
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. Here, we used restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) to link peripubertal hormone levels to individual differences in brain microarchitecture (i.e., cellular and neurite density) in 7,457 youth (ages 9 to 13 years) from the ABCD Study. Sex- and age-stratified multi-task regression analyses identified microarchitecture patterns jointly associated with physical pubertal maturation and each dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), testosterone, estradiol (in female youth), in turn, combining repeated cross-validation with permutation-based feature importance. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.

item.title: Neural processing of linguistic speech features and their modulation by selective attention in users of hearing aids and cochlear implants
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding speech relies on the neural processing of acoustic and linguistic features, which can both be analyzed using Temporal Response Functions (TRFs). While both types of features have been the focus of numerous studies in typical-hearing individuals, much less is known about the neural processing of continuous speech for people with hearing loss, particularly how hearing-impaired listeners process word-level features in noisy environments, where they typically struggle. We recorded EEG from hearing aid (HA, n=29) and cochlear implant (CI, n=24) users, and an age-matched typical-hearing (TH) control group (n=29), while participants listened to audiobook segments in quiet and with a competing speaker, using their personal hearing devices (CI and HA). A hierarchical encoding framework incrementally added word onset, word frequency, and word surprisal as predictors of the EEG signal. Attentional modulation was assessed by comparing encoding scores for attended versus ignored speech. All three groups showed clear neural responses to word onset, frequency, and surprisal for speech in quiet. Surprisal tracking emerged at 400~ms in TH participants, 500~ms in HA users, and 600~ms in CI users, weakest in the CI group. All three groups exhibited attentional modulation of surprisal tracking. Word frequency yielded significant encoding gains in quiet only for TH and HI listeners, not CI users. We show for the first time that CI users exhibit significant, attention-modulated neural responses to word surprisal. More broadly, surprisal tracking was present across all hearing-impaired groups but weakest in CI users, the cohort with the greatest difficulty understanding speech in noise.

item.title: Neural sensitivity to musical rhythm is associated with the temporal dynamics of statistical learning in speech
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Statistical learning enables the extraction of structure from the environment, including word units from continuous speech. Yet inter-individual variability suggests contributions from other, potentially broader domain-general mechanisms. Here, we investigated whether individual differences in music rhythm processing are associated with the dynamics of statistical learning during speech segmentation, potentially reflecting shared sensitivity to temporal regularities across music and language. Adults were exposed to structured and random artificial speech streams while neural tracking at syllable and word rate frequencies was tracked over time using EEG to characterize the emergence of word representations. In addition, participants’ abilities to process rhythm in musical materials were assessed using behavioral and neural (EEG) measures. Neural measurements revealed robust tracking at the syllabic level in both structured and random streams, whereas word-level tracking emerged over exposure only in the structured stream condition. Importantly, individual differences in neural synchronization to musical rhythms were associated with the temporal dynamics of word extraction. These results suggest that individual differences in the ability to process temporal regularities in musical material are related to the efficiency with which statistical regularities are extracted from sequential language material. More broadly, the findings provide evidence for domain-general mechanisms supporting sensitivity to temporal structure regularities across auditory domains.

item.title: Neural correlates of individual differences in cognition: a behavioral performance, EEG, and MRI dataset
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability. The multi-indicator design supports latent-variable modeling of all major constructs alongside their structural, functional, and electrophysiological neural correlates. Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). Electroencephalography (EEG) data was collected during four resting-state blocks and during task performance (cognitive control and processing speed). High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging using the SANDI protocol, and multi-band multi-echo functional MRI during rest and task-switching were acquired in a subset. Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data are accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository. All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.

item.title: Reconsidering the Psychotomimetic Properties of LSD: Connectome-Based Classification Reveals Partial Overlap with First Episode Psychosis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The acute effects of lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) have long been compared to early psychosis. Despite this, no studies have compared the acute effects of LSD and psychosis on resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) with parallel approaches. We used connectome-based classification, a data-driven method, to distinguish between medication-naïve, non-affective first episode psychosis (FEP) and the acute effects of LSD. Separate classifiers were trained to distinguish the acute effects of LSD from placebo and FEP patients from matched healthy controls. The LSD-placebo classifier was then validated on an external LSD-placebo dataset. The network-interaction classifiers with good discriminability were then applied across datasets to evaluate whether LSD-related connectivity patterns could classify FEP as being LSD-like and vice versa. Subsequently, we investigated univariate RSFC between select networks, based on which network-interactions the classifiers suggested might overlap in LSD and FEP. Cross-application of externally validated LSD-placebo classifiers revealed partial overlap between LSD and FEP, particularly involving the dorsal attention network (DAN) and sensorimotor network (SMN). Application of the most discriminant FEP-HC network-interaction classifiers revealed that LSD displayed select similarities with FEP. Univariate network analysis also supports between-network DAN and SMN dysconnectivity being a point of convergence. Our findings indicate that neural correlates of FEP might have select overlaps with changes in brain functioning produced by LSD. These results suggest serotonergic dysfunction might play a role in the early stages of psychosis and necessitate future studies directly comparing FEP and LSD.

item.title: Spatial trapping and anteroposterior segregation of the default mode network in schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The spatial organisation of the default mode network (DMN) across recurrent brain configurations remains poorly understood in schizophrenia. Here, we introduce two indices to quantify how selectively a network is represented across brain modes and whether selected anterior and posterior regions participate in the same configurations. Resting-state functional MRI from 16 healthy controls and 11 participants with non-acute schizophrenia was used to assess static and dynamic functional connectivity, global synchronisation, intrinsic ignition and variability measures. Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis identified the brain modes. The Spatial Trapping Index (STI) measured the distribution of relative network composition across four modes, while anterior–posterior co-participation (CAP) measured shared these modes. The two indices were compared using permutation test within Holm correction. Static functional connectivity was lower within the dorsal attention network, while dynamic functional connectivity showed greater variability in several network. No significant differences were detected in global synchronisation, intrinsic ignition or the three signatures of metastability. Mean DMN composition was similar between groups, but STI was higher in SCZ, while CAP was lower. Bootstrap resampling retained the observed directions in 89.6% of STI contrasts and 91.9% of CAP contrasts. These findings suggest that DMN representation is less selective across brain modes in schizophrenia, while selected anterior and posterior regions participate less consistently together. STI and CAP offer a new way to quantify these complementary aspects of spatial organisation, providing a basis for investigating their clinical relevance.

item.title: Saccadic network dysfunction underlies eye-movement variability in early Parkinson's disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by altered subcortical-cortical connectivity, leading to motor and cognitive deficits. Saccadic eye movement abnormalities are among the earliest and most persistent markers of the disease, serving as sensitive indicators of disrupted oculomotor and cognitive control. While changes in average saccadic behavioral measures are widely reported in Parkinson's disease, intra-individual variability in saccadic performance and the underlying network dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we quantified intra-individual saccadic variability in early-stage Parkinson’s disease and identified its functional correlates within the resting-state saccadic network. We analyzed data from the inclusion visit of 91 patients with early-stage Parkinson’s disease and 46 healthy controls from the ICEBERG cohort (monocentric prospective research study) who underwent oculomotor testing and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. First, at the behavioral level, we assessed intra-individual variability in saccadic performance within each group using the coefficient of variation of reaction time and normalized peak velocity across trials. Second, at the brain level, we assessed group differences in static and dynamic functional connectivity across 39 regions comprising the saccadic network. We examined the relationship between network connectivity and saccadic variability using partial least squares analysis. We also quantified network organization using graph-theory measures of global efficiency and clustering coefficient. Finally, we tested the relevance of intra-individual saccadic variability and network features in distinguishing patients from healthy controls using a multivariate Mahalanobis classifier. Our results showed that, compared to HC, patients had higher intra-individual variability in saccadic behavioral measures of reaction time (p Holm = 0.012) and normalized peak velocity (p Holm = 0.012). Interestingly, patients had (i) reduced static and dynamic connectivity within the saccadic network and (ii) weaker associations between network connectivity and intra-individual saccadic variability of specifically normalized peak velocity. These results were particularly driven by regions within the cognitive saccade network. The classifier that integrated intra-individual saccadic variability and network connectivity achieved 95.62% accuracy in distinguishing patients from healthy controls, with dynamic connectivity contributing more strongly to classification performance than static connectivity. We demonstrate that elevated intra-individual variability of saccades, underpinned by altered functional connectivity within cognitive-oculomotor networks, is a prominent feature of early-stage Parkinson’s disease. Emerging as a promising physiological marker of disease pathophysiology, intra-individual variability offers a powerful new framework to refine early diagnosis and improve the tracking of neurodegeneration before severe clinical milestones are reached.

item.title: Robust sex differences in regional gray matter volume but shared personality-gray matter associations in young adults.
item.description:
PloS one
Relationships between personality traits and brain regions have been widely studied, but potential sex-based differences have received less attention, despite sex hormones affecting neuronal activity and brain functions. We aimed to determine whether the personality-brain relationship differs fundamentally between the sexes. We enrolled healthy university students (103 men, 111 women). Gray matter volumes were measured in 388 brain regions using voxel-based morphometry on T1-weighted brain MRI, and personality traits were assessed using the temperament and character inventory. In confirmatory analyses correcting for multiple comparisons across all 388 regions and seven factors (Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate), main-effect sex differences in gray matter volume were robust: 17 regions survived correction, independent of personality, and were predominantly subcortical (thalamus, pallidum and putamen) and right-lateralized. By contrast, neither any association between personality and gray matter volume nor any personality-by-sex interaction survived correction, indicating that personality-gray matter associations were not detectably different between the sexes. In a cross-validated penalized regression over all regions, only self-transcendence was predicted above chance (out-of-sample R2 ≈ 0.04, permutation p = 0.004), and this prediction was essentially unchanged after adjustment for sex and total intracranial volume. In exploratory region-wise analyses (uncorrected p < 0.05), the distribution of brain regions associated with each personality factor appeared to differ between the sexes; for instance, harm avoidance in females was related mainly to parietal, temporal and thalamic regions, whereas in males it was related mainly to sensorimotor and cerebellar regions. These exploratory patterns did not survive correction and are reported as hypothesis-generating observations. Overall, sex differences in this young adult sample were robust for subcortical volume but not for the coupling between personality and gray matter volume, which appeared largely shared between the sexes, underscoring the importance of considering sex as a biological variable while distinguishing confirmed effects from exploratory observations.

item.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Functions in Patients With Essential Tremor Without Dementia: Beyond the Cerebellum.
item.description:
Neurology
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Essential tremor (ET) is characterized not only by motor disturbances but also, in many cases, by a wide array of cognitive symptoms. Accumulating evidence implicates pathways beyond the cerebellum by which cognitive changes emerge. However, the extracerebellar neuropathologic correlates of specific cognitive symptoms have not been examined. This study evaluated these potential clinicopathologic associations in older adults with ET. METHODS: Participants were adults ≥55 years with ET who were followed prospectively and longitudinally and donated their brains for neuropathologic evaluation as part of the Clinical-Pathological Study of Cognitive Impairment in Essential Tremor study. Cognitive outcomes included attention, executive function, language, memory, and visuospatial function. Postmortem neuropathologic assessment included Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) neuritic plaque scores, Thal β-amyloid A score, Braak and Braak neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) stage, and Braak Lewy pathology stage. Regional cerebral cortical atrophy ratings (neocortical and hippocampal), cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and markers of cerebrovascular health were also rated. Regression models examined neuropathologic correlates of cognitive function, adjusting for numerous confounders. Sensitivity analyses examined robustness of findings. RESULTS: The sample consisted of 57 individuals with ET and without dementia (mean age = 88.6 ± 5.4 years; 54.4% female, 71.9% cognitively normal, 28.1% with mild cognitive impairment). Higher amyloid burden was associated with lower attention (CERAD β = -0.48, p < 0.001; Thal β = -0.37, p < 0.01) and lower executive function (CERAD β = -0.40, p 0.01; Thal β = -0.33, p = 0.01). CERAD score was associated with lower language (β = -0.31, p = 0.04). Braak NFT stage was associated with lower attention (β = -0.26, p = 0.04) and lower executive function (β = -0.28, p = 0.03). Hippocampal atrophy was associated with lower memory performance (β = -0.29, p = 0.04). DISCUSSION: Core pathologies of AD, amyloid and tau, are associated with decrements in attention and executive function in older adults with ET and without dementia, while hippocampal atrophy is associated with lower memory performance. These results, consistent with a growing literature on extracerebellar pathologies in ET, suggest that multidomain cognitive symptoms among older adults with ET and without dementia may be driven in large part by AD-related cortical degenerative processes. Ongoing work is examining the molecular basis of these processes. Limitations include a highly educated, demographically homogeneous, and relatively small sample, as well as a lack of a control group.

item.title: Distinct Amygdala-Frontopolar and Amygdala-Medial Temporal Pathways Support Temporal Memory for Emotional Events.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Growing evidence suggests that emotion shapes temporal aspects of memory-such as remembering when an event occurred-yet the neural bases of these effects remain unclear. Prior work indicates that temporal context representations in memory are supported by the functions of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and prefrontal regions, including hippocampus, perirhinal cortex, and lateral frontopolar cortex (FPl). These regions have privileged access to amygdala-originated affective signals that may mediate emotional influences on temporal memory. To test whether these candidate pathways shape temporal memory for emotional events, participants encoded trial-unique negative and positive images in the scanner, followed by a surprise temporal memory task. We found that more negative stimuli were associated with greater amygdala activation and lower temporal memory error for when emotional images occurred. Replicating and extending prior work, higher stimulus-evoked multivoxel pattern similarity in the hippocampus and FPl was associated with higher temporal memory error. Notably, greater amygdala responding to emotional images predicted higher between-trial pattern similarity in the hippocampus but lower within- and between-trial similarity in FPl. Amygdala engagement was also correlated with greater perirhinal activation, which in turn predicted stronger item memory and a recency bias in temporal memory estimates. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct-and opposing-modulatory effects of amygdala-FPl and amygdala-MTL pathways on temporal memory, with the potential to sharpen and blur memory for when emotional events occurred.

item.title: Early Neural Responses to Negative Emotional Processing and Longitudinal Grief Trajectories in Later Life.
item.description:
Psychotherapy and psychosomatics
Introduction While most bereaved adults adapt to their loss within a year, 3-10% develop Prolonged Grief Disorder. The neurobiological substrates of adaptive versus maladaptive grief trajectories remain poorly understood. Methods In this longitudinal study, ninety-seven adults (50-83 years) bereaved within the past year completed task-based fMRI (an emotional face-matching paradigm) and resting-state fMRI at study baseline. Grief symptoms were repeatedly assessed over 12 months. Voxel-wise linear mixed-effects models with cluster-wise correction (uncorrected p=.005; alpha=.05) examined associations between baseline fMRI responses to negative emotional faces (fearful and angry) versus shapes and 12-month symptom trajectories, adjusting for demographics, time since loss, and depressive symptoms. Results At baseline, left anterior insula activity was positively associated with loneliness (r=.305) and intrusive thoughts (r=.328). Longitudinally, greater baseline activity in bilateral anterior insula and left amygdala was associated with faster improvement in loneliness (z<-3.01). Lower amygdala-orbitofrontal cortex resting-state connectivity was associated with faster loneliness improvement, with stronger effects at higher depressive symptoms and greater perceived social support. Conversely, greater left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity (z=3.10) and its task-dependent connectivity with lateral occipital cortices (z=3.18) were associated with slower improvement in avoidant coping. Conclusion Greater engagement of salience network circuit components during negative emotional processing was associated with diminishing loneliness, whereas greater recruitment of prefrontal executive control network node was associated with persistent avoidance. These findings suggest distinct neural pathways underlying adaptive versus maladaptive grief responses. Further research to confirm these observations and to develop early risk stratification and mechanism-informed interventions to prevent prolonged grief is needed.

item.title: Cross-domain encoding models reveal shared and domain-specific neural representations across language and mathematics.
item.description:
Science advances
Whether language and mathematics rely on shared or distinct neural representations remains unresolved in cognitive neuroscience. Here, we combined latent features from a large language model with functional magnetic resonance imaging encoding models to test cross-domain generalization in 32 participants performing sentence comprehension and calculation tasks. Cross-domain prediction identified cortical regions showing partially shared representations, most consistently in the left area 55b, while control analyses suggested that these effects could not be fully explained by low-level visual or task-general factors. Domain-specificity contrasts revealed stronger language-related prediction in the left superior temporal sulcus and angular gyrus and math-related prediction in the left precentral sulcus and bilateral intraparietal sulci. Model-weight analyses revealed distinct weight profiles associated with shared and domain-specific prediction patterns. Cross-domain regions also exhibited task-dependent functional coupling with language- and math-related networks. Together, these findings suggest that language and mathematics involve partially shared neural representations alongside domain-specific cortical organization, helping reconcile previous contrasting views on their neural basis.

item.title: Auditory cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulations is sufficient to support perceptual categorization of speech and music.
item.description:
Science advances
Auditory processing is typically described as hierarchical, culminating in neural representation of abstract categories. However, it remains unclear whether category-selective responses in auditory cortex require representational mechanisms beyond the coding of acoustic features or whether the acoustic representations already available in the auditory cortex are sufficient to account for categorization. Here, we test whether cortical coding of spectrotemporal modulation (STM) features is sufficient to support speech-music categorization by combining human intracranial recordings with continuous behavioral judgments of a naturalistic soundtrack in which speech and music occur both separately and simultaneously. We show that temporal and spectral modulation patterns largely characterize speech and music, respectively, and that cortical auditory regions robustly track these features over time, with distinct oscillatory frequency bands preferentially encoding temporal and spectral modulations. Critically, cortical representations of STMs predicted perceptual categorical judgments gathered in an independent sample. Last, speech- and music-related STM representations showed stronger tracking of category-specific acoustical features in left versus right cortical auditory regions, respectively. These findings indicate that the efficient neural coding of acoustical features provides a sufficient basis for the categorical distinction between speech and music and that the temporal and spectral components of this representation are implemented through distinct oscillatory mechanisms.

item.title: The hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine for memory, perception and cognitive dysfunction.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
The hippocampus is a central cognitive hub whose dysfunction contributes to most neurodegenerative dementias. Despite extensive knowledge of its anatomy, physiology and circuitry, a unifying account that links hippocampal dynamics to cognition and clinical syndromes remains lacking. Drawing on systems neuroscience and recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, we conceptualize the hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine that compresses sensory, interoceptive and cognitive inputs into low-dimensional representations and regenerates percepts, episodic memories and imagined scenes for cortical integration. Travelling waves of cortico-hippocampal oscillations, aligned with large-scale functional gradients, schedule and structure this generative process and organize distributed neural activity into coherent, semantically grounded constructs. We formalize this proposal as stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion (SLOD), a biologically grounded framework that maps hippocampal-cortical computations onto specific anatomical substrates and dynamical processes. While we do not suggest that the hippocampus implements diffusion algorithms per se, we show that its computations can be decomposed into homologous operations including compression, stochastic exploration, conditioning and reconstruction, whose formal structure closely parallels that of latent diffusion models. Finally, we demonstrate how major neurodegenerative dementias, including the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia, can be understood as selective breakdowns of distinct components of this generative architecture.

item.title: Reverberant magnetic resonance elastography and NODDI provide complementary characterization of age-related brain changes in healthy adults.
item.description:
Physics in medicine and biology
Objective. Age-related changes in brain microstructure and mechanical properties are essential for understanding neurodegeneration and improving early diagnosis. We asked whether tissue microstructure explains the age-related decline in brain stiffness. To test, we related stiffness, measured using reverberant magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), to microstructure, assessed by neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI).Approach. Twenty-eight healthy volunteers (22-76 years) underwent 50 Hz MRE at 3 T. NODDI parameters (isotropic volume fraction Fiso; orientation dispersion index, ODI; neurite density index, NDI) were computed from diffusion-weighted images in 26 subjects. We analyzed global gray and white matter and 13 deep brain regions. Age associations were evaluated using Spearman correlations. Multivariate regression was used to test whether NODDI parameters predicted shear modulus independently of age. All tests used Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction.Main results. Shear modulus decreased with age in both gray matter (,) and white matter (,), and in nine of 13 deep brain regions after FDR correction. Fiso (,) and NDI (,) increased with age in gray matter; no NODDI parameter changed significantly with age in white matter. Across the six global multivariate tests (gray and white matterthree NODDI parameters), only the gray-matter Fiso independently predicted shear modulus after adjusting for age (,); no NODDI parameter predicted white matter stiffness. This association did not survive FDR correction after additional adjustment for sex ().Significance. These findings suggest that cortical free water accumulation is the microstructural measure most closely associated with age-related softening in this cohort, pending confirmation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts, and support a multi-modal approach to characterizing age-related brain changes.

item.title: An electrophysiological investigation of inhibitory control in children with dyslexia and the role of comorbid ADHD symptoms: a pilot randomized intervention study.
item.description:
Child neuropsychology : a journal on normal and abnormal development in childhood and adolescence
Neurobiological research indicates that atypical functioning within left-hemisphere parietal and temporal regions is associated with word-processing difficulties in children with dyslexia. This study used event-related potentials (ERPs) to examine the neural correlates of inhibitory control in children with dyslexia, the effects of computerized inhibition training, and the influence of ADHD symptoms. This pilot study employed a randomized, double-blind, dosage-controlled intervention design. Participants were 62 children aged 10-12 years, including 37 children with dyslexia and 25 typically-developing controls (TDCs). Intervention analyses included 34 children with dyslexia assigned to high (n = 18) or low-dose (n = 16) training. Behavioral performance, electrophysiological responses during a Go/No-Go task, and ADHD symptoms were assessed. Independent samples t-tests showed that children with dyslexia exhibited significantly slower reaction times than TDCs during the picture Go/No-Go task. Children with dyslexia also demonstrated reduced left-lateralized N2 and P3 amplitudes over fronto-central and fronto-temporal regions relative to TDCs at baseline. ADHD inattentive symptoms were significantly associated with slower reaction times at baseline. Mixed-factorial ANOVAs revealed significant reductions in reaction times across both training groups, together with pre- to post-intervention changes in several N2 and P3 indices. These findings suggest that children with dyslexia exhibit altered neural correlates of inhibitory control despite relatively modest behavioral differences and highlight the importance of considering ADHD symptomatology when investigating executive functioning in dyslexia.

item.title: [Cognitive involvement in adult myotonic dystrophy type 1: new findings from the North].
item.description:
Medecine sciences : M/S
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is the most common adult-onset myopathy, but is also a brain disorder leading to cognitive impairment. This brain condition remains poorly characterized: the scientific literature highlighted different cognitive profiles, and no predominant mechanism has been identified. Recent findings from our team in Lille, France, help to better understand this cognitive impairment. We showed that three distinct cognitive profiles exist, patients probably starting from the least severe to the most severe profile with ageing, while brain abnormalities progress in the anterior regions of the brain (frontal and parietal lobes). Despite this cognitive heterogeneity, some difficulties seemed more frequent in our patients, especially those concerning social cognition (skills especially involved in social interactions), and might be explained by white matter lesions in the temporal poles, but also by neurodevelopmental abnormalities in the right parietal lobe.

item.title: Microstructure regulation of Co3O4via a variable temperature strategy for efficient azo dye degradation by peroxymonosulfate activation.
item.description:
Dalton transactions (Cambridge, England : 2003)
Peroxymonosulfate (PMS)-activated advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) are promising for the removal of refractory azo dyes, and the catalytic performance of Co3 O4 strongly depends on its surface and microstructural characteristics. Herein, Co3 O4 microspheres were prepared by a solvothermal-annealing route, and their microstructures were regulated by varying the annealing temperature from 350 to 650 °C without changing the spinel phase. Increasing the annealing temperature induced progressive nanoparticle coarsening and decreased the BET specific surface area from 7.68 m2 g-1 for Co3 O4 -350 to 1.08 m2 g-1 for Co3 O4 -650. Among the samples, Co3 O4 -350 exhibited the highest PMS activation activity, achieving 99.1% removal of Ponceau Red 2R (PR) within 3 min with an apparent pseudo-first-order rate constant of 1.6693 min-1 . Quantitative comparison with representative Co3 O4 -based PMS activation systems reported in the literature further demonstrates the competitive kinetic performance of Co3 O4 -350, with a catalyst-mass-normalized apparent rate constant of 5.5643 L g-1 min-1 . Radical quenching experiments and EPR measurements support the involvement of SO4 ˙- , ˙OH, O2 ˙- , and 1 O2 in the oxidation process. Co3 O4 -350 also retained 93.7% PR removal after eight consecutive cycles. These results show that simple annealing-temperature regulation can effectively tune the accessible surface structure of compositionally unmodified Co3 O4 and provide a competitive route for PMS activation toward azo-dye degradation.

item.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Nature
Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

item.title: The Tapetum: Historical Evolution, Anatomical Insights, and Contemporary Neurosurgical Relevance.
item.description:
World neurosurgery
OBJECTIVE: The tapetum is a thin commissural fiber layer originating predominantly from the splenium of the corpus callosum and forming part of the lateral wall of the atrium and temporal horn of the lateral ventricle. Although surgically relevant, its historical development has received limited attention. This review examines the evolution of the anatomical concept of the tapetum from early descriptions of interhemispheric and ventricular anatomy to contemporary fiber-dissection and tractographic perspectives. METHODS: A narrative historical review was conducted using classical neuroanatomical texts from the sixteenth to twentieth centuries and contemporary studies identified through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Historical primary sources and modern anatomical, surgical, and imaging studies were reviewed. RESULTS: Early concepts of interhemispheric connectivity arose from descriptions of the corpus callosum and ventricular anatomy. Johann Christian Reil formally defined the tapetum in 1809 as a carpet-like layer of callosal fibers lining the lateral ventricular wall. Nineteenth-century anatomists, including Burdach, Arnold, Gratiolet, Flechsig, Meynert, and the Dejerines, refined its topography while highlighting uncertainties regarding adjacent projection and association pathways. Twentieth-century fiber dissection, particularly the Klingler method, enabled three-dimensional visualization, while modern diffusion imaging and tractography supported the interpretation of the tapetum as a thin laminar extension of splenial callosal fibers. CONCLUSION: The tapetum concept evolved from descriptive ventricular anatomy to a fiber-based understanding of posterior interhemispheric connectivity. Its close relationship with the optic radiation and lateral ventricular wall underscores its relevance in contemporary approaches to the atrium and temporal horn.

item.title: Brain volumes and their relationship with cerebral microbleeds and cognition in middle-aged adults with type 1 diabetes.
item.description:
Diabetes research and clinical practice
AIMS: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is associated with brain volumetric alterations, cerebral microbleeds (CMBs), and cognitive deficits. We examined brain volumes and their direct and combined associations with CMBs on cognitive performance in T1D. METHODS: Adults with T1D (n = 163; age 46 ± 8 years; diabetes duration 31 ± 10 years; 53% women) and 48 matched controls underwent brain MRI and clinical and neuropsychological evaluations. Volumetric MRI measures included total brain (TBV) and white matter volume (WMV), and volumes of cortex, thalamus, hippocampus, nucleus accumbens, and choroid plexus. RESULTS: Individuals with T1D had smaller TBV, WMV, cortex, thalamus, and nucleus accumbens volumes, and larger choroid plexus, than controls (Cohen's d = 0.39-0.54). Those with T1D and ≥3 CMBs (n = 25) had smaller TBV, WMV, and cortex, thalamus, and nucleus accumbens than those with 0-2 CMBs (n = 138; Cohen's d = 0.54-0.92). Brain volumes were not directly linked to cognition, but CMB burden moderated the associations between TBV, WMV, nucleus accumbens, and choroid plexus and cognitive performance (standardized β: -0.61-(-0.51) and 0.54-0.75, pFDR = 0.006-0.048). CONCLUSIONS: Middle-aged individuals with T1D showed smaller global and regional brain volumes and larger choroid plexus than healthy controls. Individuals with CMB burden showed associations between brain volumetric alterations and cognitive deficits.

item.title: Remodeling stress-responsive networks following early life adversity: Insights from preclinical models.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Early life adversity (ELA) is a leading risk factor for the development of mental illness worldwide. While the association between experiencing developmental stress and psychopathology is robust, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from clinical and preclinical studies suggests that ELA may hijack typical developmental plasticity mechanisms, leading to maladaptive functional network changes. Understanding the nature and magnitude of these changes is complicated by several key dimensions, including the timing, type, and severity of ELA, as well as biological factors such as sex and genetic makeup. Preclinical models using primates and rodents have allowed for fine control over these variables, providing substantial evidence of pathways and related biomarkers impacted by ELA. The present review aims to bridge findings from human clinical data with preclinical research, highlighting well-supported ELA-induced changes in the functional connectivity of stress-sensitive pathways, as well as alterations in additional cortical and subcortical pathways which are susceptible to disturbances during development. We also present key neuromodulatory mechanisms contributing to connectivity changes observed in preclinical models, and sex-specific nuances. Addressing these critical gaps could enhance the potential of connectivity-based therapeutic approaches. Lastly, we consider the translatability of functional connectivity analyses using various preclinical techniques for studying the influence of ELA on the developing brain.

item.title: Transcriptional Patterns of Disruption in Structure-Function Coupling in First-episode, Drug-naive Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience bulletin
First-episode major depressive disorder (FEMDD) is associated with alterations in macroscale brain organization, which may involve changes in brain structure-function coupling (SFC). Whether alterations in SFC affect the emergence of depression and how they correlate with gene expression remain unclear. Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were collected from 95 healthy controls and 124 patients with FEMDD. We applied SFC analysis to calculate the structural decoupling index (SDI) and to quantify SFC in the two groups. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between alterations in SDI and gene expression. The FEMDD group showed a significantly lower SDI in the inferior frontal gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, medial orbital gyrus, pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, and lateral occipital cortex (LOcC), whereas a significantly higher SDI was observed in the inferior temporal gyrus, lateral superior frontal gyrus, medial precuneus, and hypergranular insula than in the healthy control group. The speed of processing and working memory scores of the Measurement and Treatment Research to Improve Cognition in Schizophrenia (MATRICS) Consensus Cognitive Battery negatively correlated with the LOcC SDI in the FEMDD group. Additionally, changes in FEMDD-related SDI were associated with the expression of genes involved in synaptic signaling and neuronal development. These findings reveal regional- and network-level alterations in structure-function coupling in patients with FEMDD, providing new insights into the neurobiological underpinnings and promising neuroimaging markers for the prediction of FEMDD.

item.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication.
item.description:
eLife
The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f ) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f 4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

item.title: Genetic, neural and early-environmental architecture of resilience
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Resilience is shaped by factors ranging from the genome through early-life experience to the brain, yet its biological basis in humans remains unclear because studies have rarely integrated these levels and have been confined to small samples. Using the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS) and multimodal data from tens of thousands of UK Biobank (UKB) participants, with replication in Generation Scotland (GS), we found that resting-state functional connectivity, particularly within the flexibility and valuation networks, is a robust neural correlate of resilience. Resilience also showed a generalizable genetic basis: a polygenic score (PGS) derived from a UKB genome-wide association study predicted BRS in GS. Genes and childhood experiences converged on the flexibility network through distinct routes: the polygenic association with resilience was partly explained by central executive-salience integration, whereas childhood experiences were associated with default-mode-centered integration. By separating genetically anchored from experience-sensitive routes, these findings point to network targets that interventions could tailor to the sources of an individual's vulnerability.

item.title: Reduced Resting Brain Entropy and Structural-Functional Reorganization in Hearing Loss
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Hearing loss changes how the brain processes sound, yet how chronic auditory degradation shapes the temporal organization of spontaneous cortical activity remains unclear. We examined this question using multimodal MRI from 52 adults with age-related hearing loss and 30 normal-hearing controls. Guided by convergent neuroimaging evidence, we focused on the superior temporal gyrus (STG) and assessed brain entropy (BEN), complementary resting-state measures, and gray matter volume (GMV). Hearing loss was associated with lower BEN in a focal right-STG cluster after adjustment for local GMV (14 voxels; cluster FWER p = 0.008), consistent with more recurrent BOLD signal patterns. Six complementary measures of signal amplitude, local synchrony, symbolic sequence diversity, successive variation, and temporal persistence showed no corrected STG differences. A separate whole-brain analysis revealed higher bilateral midcingulate cortex (MCC) GMV (FWE p = 0.002 and 0.015), motivating examination of the auditory-cingulate relationship. The BEN-defined STG region showed stronger focal functional connectivity with MCC (FWE p = 0.031). Exploratory analyses suggested weaker directed STG-to-MCC influence alongside a small tractography-derived group difference. Exploratory directional comparisons indicated stronger right-MCC GMV-BEN coupling (p = 0.034) and STG-MCC SC-FC coupling (p = 0.037) in controls than in hearing loss. Together, these findings link greater temporal regularity in auditory association cortex to altered auditory-cingulate coordination and local structure-function correspondence, suggesting that adaptation to hearing loss involves both the organization of spontaneous cortical dynamics and their relationship to brain structure.

item.title: ACC Sulcal Morphology as a Neurodevelopmental Marker of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Control among Adolescents
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. BI has been linked to variation in cognitive control, particularly proactive control, a crucial component of executive functions which involves monitoring one's own behavior and adapting that behavior to achieve a particular goal, which may help explain BI's association with elevated anxiety risk. Yet little is known about the neurobiology of cognitive control development among children with BI. Variation in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sulcal pattern asymmetry, established prenatally and stable across development, is associated with individual differences in cognitive control. This preliminary study examined whether ACC sulcal symmetry is associated with BI, proactive and reactive control (measured via the AX-CPT) in adolescents. Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired from 62 adolescents aged 12 to 15 years. ACC patterns in each hemisphere were classified as 'single type' or 'double parallel type' based on the presence of a paracingulate sulcus. Adolescents with symmetric ACC patterns showed lower proactive control ( d ′ context; η 2 p = .091) and greater reactive control (BX probe interference effect; η 2 p = .119). These associations held even when tested within the same statistical model and were comparable in magnitude. ACC symmetry was not associated with BI, nor did it interact with BI to predict cognitive control scores. Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence that ACC sulcal morphology may be a structural marker of variability in cognitive control, with relevance to BI-related neurocognitive risk.

item.title: Dance experience shapes local brain dynamics and shared responses during naturalistic action observation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. Dance expertise is known to alter action-related activation and the similarity of spectators' responses, but its association with local BOLD dynamics during an extended performance remains unclear. We reanalyzed fMRI from 14 professional dancers and 11 novices watching the same 33-minute dance film; one choreographer provided a separate reference. In the first 678 volumes, we measured voxelwise brain entropy (BEN) using sample entropy before summarizing it in Schaefer 400 parcels and seven networks, calculated windowed entropy from parcel-mean signals, and examined intersubject correlation (ISC) and four group-blind coactivation patterns (CAPs). After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

item.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective: Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. Methods: We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. Results: Combined saccade vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7 to 49.3%; p=0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. Conclusions: These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. Significance: Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

item.title: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

item.title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Voxel-wise group comparisons and partial least squares correlation analyses examined brain-behavior associations across a comprehensive behavioral battery spanning reading (e.g., word reading, phonological processing), math, oral language, working memory, and executive function domains. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

item.title: Social Connection: Resting-State Functional Connectivity Associations with Social Networks, and the Roles of Empathy and Sex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Smaller social networks (SNs) negatively influence cognition, psychiatric trajectories and mortality. Studies linking SNs to resting-state functional connectivity (FC) inconsistently suggest orbito-frontal and frontoparietal regions and implicate a potential role for empathy and sex. We investigate how SN characteristics relate to FC, additionally assessing if empathy and sex alter these associations. Group-independent component analysis was applied to multi-band resting-state fMRI from 83 participants (Caltech Conte dataset: ds003798). The Social Network Index measures SN-contacts (SN-contacts) SN-diversity (number of roles) and SN-embeddedness (number of contact groups) and the Empathy Quotient measured empathy. Using MANCOVA, we investigate if resting-state network power and connectivity are associated with SNI measures and whether these relationships differ by empathizing ability and sex. Participants aged 18-48 (mean age 29.3+/-7.0, 55% male) demonstrated SN-contacts and SN-diversity associated with lower frontal-pole FC within the default-mode network (DMN, q-values<0.05). Empathy altered how SN-diversity and SN-contacts relate to superior lateral-occipital, default mode and salience network FC (q-values<0.05). Finally, males and females showed diverging associations of SN-contacts and SN-diversity with salience network power. Smaller SNs were associated with increased anterior-DMN FC, potentially indicating a tendency towards internally-directed cognition in more socially isolated individuals. Opposing relationships between SNs with salience and lateral-frontoparietal networks by empathy level highlights empathy as critical for understanding social biology. Males and females differed in SN associations with salience network coherency, supporting known sex-specific neural correlates of social behavior. These findings provide insights into the biology of social networks, offering potential targets for studying social deficits in psychiatric populations.

item.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

item.title: Advances in Neuroscience in an Age of Rapid Technological and AI Innovation – Towards Integration Across Scales
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Rapid technological innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed not only the resolution at which the brain can be observed, but also the questions that can be asked, shifting the field from description toward prediction, regulation and generation. Yet progress has largely advanced along parallel trajectories, and findings at one level rarely inform or constrain the next. Here, we review recent advances in three exemplary domains and propose a future-oriented framework for their integration. First, molecular and cellular neurotechnology, including synaptic proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution microscopy, optoacoustic and ultrasound imaging, sonogenetics and molecular MRI, resolves neural processes with unprecedented specificity. Second, AI-based decoding of human brain activity yields precise signatures of complex, subjective conscious experiences in naturalistic contexts and is beginning to inform diagnosis, drug evaluation and individualized neuromodulation in mental disorders. Third, large-scale neural recordings, mechanistic whole-brain simulations, neural foundation models and AI surrogate brains are converging toward individualized digital twin brains. We argue that the next level of progress requires integrating these domains into a closed loop of reciprocal constraints, in which molecular measurements inform model parameters, human signatures define and evaluate what models must reproduce, and model predictions prioritize perturbations that can be tested across domains.
